rv.q: Mindell’s play often feels like one of those ill-fated kitchen endeavors where a dish comes out burnt on the outside and raw in the middle, somehow both over- and underbaked.
Earnest, thoughtful, and full of the most existential themes, this is a play that will be tugging at your heartstrings before you can say “evolutionary function of shame.”
While its writing and staging don't always do justice to its profound themes, its message remains undeniable: there is beauty in difference, and in the hard-fought challenges that shape us.
The play engages our minds with its ideas but not our hearts with its emotions.
Despite its willingness to hit certain nerves On the Evolutionary Function of Shame is a tyro work, shaped by aspirations it can't fully meet.
In all, Mindell is to be congratulated and thanked for a fervent screed on behalf of continuing trans presence, even though his energetic fervor often obscures his theatrical vision.
This contemporary tale is a smorgasbord of ideas that will accompany you for a long, long time.

Still, there are moments when the characters can seem less like recognizable individuals than mouthpieces for a particular line of argument.

cn.t: Mindell's ambitious play exploring trans identity through parallel biblical and futuristic narratives earns mixed reviews. Critics praise its timeliness and moving themes, but find the execution uneven and not fully worked out.
